passages.summary: God appoints Jeremiah to speak to nations. Jeremiah objects that he is young and cannot speak. God answers Jeremiah’s fear with a promise of presence. The call includes both tearing down and building.

passages.title: Broken water tanks and abandoned loyalty
passages.summary: Jeremiah recalls Israel’s early loyalty and later worship of other gods. He challenges reliance on Egypt and Assyria. A broken water tank cannot hold the water people need. The comparison questions choices that leave Israel without reliable help.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me compares God’s help with living water. What makes the broken water tanks poor replacements?

passages.title: An invitation to return
passages.summary: God compares Israel and Judah with unfaithful wives. He calls scattered people to return and promises caring leaders. The marriage comparison accuses the nations of broken loyalty. The invitation still offers return rather than permanent rejection.

passages.title: An approaching enemy and a ruined land
passages.summary: Jeremiah warns of an army coming from the north. He pictures the land without light, people, or fruitful fields. The ruined landscape reverses the ordered world of creation. Jeremiah’s grief shows what the threatened destruction would cost.

passages.title: A search for justice
passages.summary: Jeremiah searches Jerusalem for someone who acts justly. He finds wrongdoing among poor people, leaders, prophets, and priests. Powerful people know the law but still reject it. The search prevents readers from blaming only the poor.

passages.title: Warnings that people refuse to hear
passages.summary: An enemy threatens Jerusalem. Leaders promise peace while people reject warnings and refuse to walk the older good path. The claim of peace hides wounds that need attention. Jeremiah compares ignored correction with metal that cannot be cleaned.

passages.title: Temple worship and harm to neighbors
passages.summary: Jeremiah challenges people who trust the temple while harming others. Families also make offerings to the queen of the sky. The building cannot protect people who exploit their neighbors. Data Over Dogma notes that men, children, and women prepare the offerings together.

passages.title: Rejected warnings and grief for the wounded
passages.summary: Jeremiah describes people refusing to return and scribes distorting the law. He grieves as harvest ends without deliverance. Knowing the law has not produced careful action. The unanswered question about healing expresses grief rather than easy reassurance.

passages.title: Broken trust and reasons for grief
passages.summary: Jeremiah mourns a people who lie and betray neighbors. He urges boasting in knowing God rather than wealth or strength. Repeated lies make even friendships unsafe. Knowing God appears through kindness and justice rather than social rank.
passages.uncertainty: Map points locate named places. Lines connect stated movements where the passage gives endpoints.

lds.text: What replaces wealth, wisdom, and strength as a reason for praise?

passages.title: Made idols and the living God
passages.summary: Jeremiah contrasts idols made from wood and metal with God. He mourns ruined homes and asks for measured correction. People must carry the objects that they made. Their inability to move supports the challenge to trusting them.

passages.title: A broken covenant and threats from Anathoth
passages.summary: God condemns Judah’s broken agreement and worship of Baal. Jeremiah learns that people from Anathoth plan to kill him. People from Jeremiah’s own community threaten him for speaking God’s message. They demand his silence rather than change their conduct.

passages.title: Jeremiah questions the success of wrongdoers
passages.summary: Jeremiah asks why dishonest people prosper. God warns about betrayal within his family and describes the ruined land. Jeremiah’s question joins personal danger with public injustice. The answer prepares him for greater strain rather than immediate relief.

passages.title: A ruined waistband and stubborn habits
passages.summary: Jeremiah buries a linen waistband and retrieves it ruined. God compares Judah’s pride and stubborn conduct with ruined cloth. The waistband once stayed close to its wearer. passages.title: Drought and competing messages
passages.summary: Drought leaves people and animals without water. Jeremiah pleads for help while other prophets deny coming war and hunger. The prophets’ reassurance conflicts with visible suffering and Jeremiah’s warning. Their claim cannot remove the danger facing those who believe them.

passages.title: Jeremiah’s suffering and renewed task
passages.summary: God rejects further pleading for Judah and recalls Manasseh’s wrongdoing. Jeremiah describes isolation and receives a renewed charge to speak. passages.title: Missing celebrations and pursuing hunters
passages.summary: God forbids Jeremiah to marry or join mourning and feasts. He describes scattering, return, and fishers and hunters pursuing people. Jeremiah’s missing household and celebrations show coming loss. The fishers and hunters pursue people whose wrongdoing God sees.

passages.title: Trust, hidden motives, and the Sabbath
passages.summary: Jeremiah contrasts trust in human strength with trust in God. He warns against carrying burdens through Jerusalem’s gates on the Sabbath. A tree near water can survive heat without losing fruit. The comparison explains steady dependence rather than a life without difficulty.

passages.summary: Jeremiah watches a potter remake spoiled clay. Opponents plan to silence him, and he asks God to punish them. The potter’s changed work explains how a nation’s conduct affects its future. Jeremiah’s later prayer expresses anger at people seeking his death.

passages.summary: Jeremiah takes elders to the Hinnom Valley and breaks a jar. He condemns child sacrifice and warns of siege and death. Unlike the soft clay, the broken jar cannot be remade. The act presents a warning of destruction that has become unavoidable.

passages.title: Pashhur attacks Jeremiah
passages.summary: Pashhur strikes Jeremiah and puts him in stocks. Jeremiah warns him of exile, praises God, and curses his own birth. Jeremiah cannot silence the message even when speaking brings shame. His praise does not erase his anguish or wish never to have lived.

passages.title: Kings judged by their treatment of others
passages.summary: Jeremiah condemns unpaid labor and violence under Judah’s kings. He contrasts Jehoiakim’s grand house with Josiah’s care for poor people. Fine cedar does not make a ruler just. Josiah’s defense of needy people gives a different measure of knowing God.

passages.title: Harmful leaders and prophets who promise peace
passages.summary: God condemns leaders who scatter people and promises a just ruler. Jeremiah challenges prophets who give false comfort and report invented dreams. The prophets’ words encourage people to continue harming others. A useful message would turn them from those actions.

passages.title: Two baskets of figs
passages.summary: God compares deported Judeans with good figs. He compares Zedekiah and those left in Judah or Egypt with spoiled figs. Being taken away does not mean God has abandoned the captives. The good figs challenge the remaining rulers’ claim to safety.

passages.title: Babylon’s rule and the cup of anger
passages.summary: Jeremiah recounts twenty-three years of ignored warnings. He announces seventy years of Babylonian rule and judgment against many nations. passages.title: Jeremiah faces a death charge
passages.summary: Priests and prophets demand Jeremiah’s death after his temple warning. Officials spare him, while Jehoiakim has another prophet, Uriah, killed. Remembering Micah’s warning helps people defend Jeremiah. Uriah’s death shows that similar speech does not guarantee the same outcome.

passages.title: A yoke warns against rebellion
passages.summary: Jeremiah wears a wooden yoke and urges rulers to serve Babylon. He rejects promises that temple vessels will soon return. A yoke joins animals for pulling loads. Jeremiah uses it to show the burden of Babylon’s rule.

passages.title: A letter to people in exile
passages.summary: Jeremiah tells captives to build homes and seek Babylon’s peace. He rejects other prophets’ claims and answers Shemaiah’s attempt to silence him. The promised future includes a long wait and ordinary work. Seeking the city’s peace helps people live during that wait.

passages.title: Healing after national suffering
passages.summary: God promises Israel and Judah return, healing, and renewed life. He also says the nations that plundered them will face loss. The wounded people have no help from former allies. The promise addresses both their injuries and their loss of belonging.

passages.title: Return and a law written in hearts
passages.summary: God promises to gather scattered people and comfort Rachel’s grief. He announces a new covenant, an agreement with Israel and Judah. God offers forgiveness and writes his law in people’s hearts. Knowing God becomes part of the restored relationship.

passages.summary: God promises to heal Jerusalem and restore joy and worship. He promises a just ruler from David’s family and continued priestly service. Wedding songs and working shepherds describe restored daily life. The ruler’s justice makes that future more than a repaired city.

passages.summary: Jerusalem’s owners release Hebrew servants under an agreement. They then force them back into service, and Jeremiah announces punishment. The owners undo freedom that they publicly promised before God. Their broken promise takes away the servants’ ability to leave.

passages.summary: Jeremiah announces destruction across Moab and captivity for Chemosh’s worshipers. He mourns ruined vineyards and ends with a promise of return. Moab’s wealth and ease cannot prevent loss. Grief for the victims remains beside the charge of pride.

passages.title: Warnings against neighboring peoples

guides.title: Study Jeremiah
guides.description: Follow selected chapters through the book.

steps.title: Jeremiah receives his call
steps.text: God appoints Jeremiah to speak to nations. Jeremiah objects that he is young and cannot speak. God answers Jeremiah’s fear with a promise of presence. The call includes both tearing down and building.

steps.title: A yoke warns against rebellion
steps.text: Jeremiah wears a wooden yoke and urges rulers to serve Babylon. He rejects promises that temple vessels will soon return. A yoke joins animals for pulling loads. Jeremiah uses it to show the burden of Babylon’s rule.

steps.title: Jerusalem’s destruction and Jehoiachin’s release
steps.text: The closing account describes Jerusalem’s siege, destruction, executions, and forced removal of captives. Years later, Evilmerodach frees Jehoiachin and gives him a daily allowance. Invaders break and carry away Solomon’s temple furnishings. Jehoiachin’s changed treatment offers limited hope without reversing the destruction.

textRoutes.detail: The promised future includes a long wait and ordinary work. Seeking the city’s peace helps people live during that wait.
